newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Semis - Retain underperforming bias.
newsitem.headline: Australian Semis - Retain underperforming bias.

text.p: *Bursts of outright buying by offshore investors in semi-government bonds in the past two weeks failed to prevent the market underperforming against Australian Treasury bonds.
Bursts of outright buying by offshore investors in semi-government bonds in the past two weeks failed to prevent the market underperforming against Australian Treasury bonds.
Traders said semis are still prone to profit-taking after the strong outperformance earlier this year, although for yield seekers, are providing a larger return as local yields shrink.

There was no immediate impact on news on Tuesday that Australia's High Court had upheld a challenge against the right of states and territories to levy excise duties, although it slightly tainted the recent bullish tone of the market.

Australia's constitution bans states and territories from levying excise, although media reports said the national government has a A$5.0 billion emergency tax package drafted to replace a string of state charges if the court upheld the challenge.
"If that is the case, the result is no net impact (from the tax change)," said one trader.
At the same time, the Victorian state government criticised the Federal government's decision to tighten tax laws on the sale of assets by tax exempt organisations.

The protest follows action on Monday by Australian Treasurer Peter Costello to close a depreciation tax loophole that allowed state governments to structure trade sale of assets to reduce company tax for buyers and lift the sale price of the assets.
Victorian Treasurer, Alan Stockdale said the changes to the depreciation rules would hurt the state's remaining electricity asset sales.
"The Commonwealth's tax grab will mean a loss of several hundred million dollars for Victorian taxpayers," he said.
Meanwhile, long-dated government bond yields fell to their lowest level since the early 1970's last week after the Reserve Bank cut official interest rates to 5.0 percent.
Yields have subsequently risen in the wake of a huge sell-off in U.S. Treasuries last Friday, although more positive domestic fundamentals is taming the local reaction.

The jury is still out as to whether this will be the last easing by the RBA in the current business cycle, but data since the policy change has remained on the weak side, and although Thursday's labour force data is expected to show some growth in employment, it will fall short of a full recovery.
